//! A tiny key-value store used by the examples.
use std::collections::HashMap;

pub struct Store {
    entries: HashMap<String, String>,
    max_entries: usize,
}

impl Store {
    pub fn new(max_entries: usize) -> Store {
        Store { entries: HashMap::new(), max_entries }
    }

    pub fn insert(&mut self, key: &str, value: &str) -> Result<(), StoreError> {
        if self.entries.len() >= self.max_entries {
            return Err(StoreError::Full);
        }
        self.entries.insert(key.to_string(), value.to_string());
        Ok(())
    }

    pub fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<&String> {
        self.entries.get(key)
    }

    pub fn remove(&mut self, key: &str) -> Option<String> {
        self.entries.remove(key)
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn insert_and_get_round_trip() {
        let mut store = Store::new(4);
        store.insert("alpha", "1").unwrap();
        store.insert("beta", "2").unwrap();
        assert_eq!(store.get("alpha").map(String::as_str), Some("1"));
        assert_eq!(store.get("gamma"), None);
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_full_store_rejects_new_entries() {
        let mut store = Store::new(1);
        store.insert("alpha", "1").unwrap();
        assert!(store.insert("beta", "2").is_err());
    }
}

# Storing small values

The store keeps every entry in memory, so it is meant for small values. Inserting a key
that already exists replaces its value; inserting into a full store is an error and
changes nothing. Keys are compared as bytes, so `Alpha` and `alpha` are different keys.

Things to know:

- The limit is set when the store is created and cannot change afterwards.
- Reading never blocks and never allocates beyond the returned reference.
- There is no persistence: when the process ends, the entries are gone.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

for file in src/*.rs; do
    if grep -q "TODO" "$file"; then
        echo "found TODO in $file"
    fi
done

count=$(find src -name '*.rs' | wc -l)
echo "checked ${count} files"
